unique_operations.before: 2.1 The Gaussian expectation maps needed in the population recurrences are Lipschitz functions of the three entries of their bivariate covariance on any region $v\le Q_{ii},Q_{jj}\le Q$, where $v>0$ is fixed. This applies to $E[g(U)g(V)]$ for $g=\sigma$ and $g=\sigma'$, and to the residual marginal map $s\mapsto E\sigma(\sqrt s Z)$. At fixed $\rho$, changing $s,t$ changes these expectations by at most $C(|\Delta s|+|\Delta t|)$: use the Lipschitz constants $L,\beta$, $s,t\ge v$, and [F5] to bound the resulting products. For fixed $s,t$ and $|\rho|<1$, the covariance matrix is positive definite, so [F7] supplies the density $\phi_{s,t,\rho}$. On any compact interval $|\rho|\le r<1$, its eigenvalues lie between $v(1-r)$ and $Q(1+r)$. Direct differentiation of the Gaussian density gives $\partial_\rho\phi_{s,t,\rho}=\sqrt{st}\,\partial_u\partial_v\phi_{s,t,\rho}$. Uniform eigenvalue bounds imply that $|g(u)g(v)\partial_\rho\phi_{s,t,\rho}(u,v)|$ is bounded by an integrable polynomial times $e^{-c(u^2+v^2)}$, uniformly on this interval; $g$ has at most linear growth and $g'$ is bounded. Thus [F8] justifies differentiating the expectation under the integral. On finite rectangles apply [F9] successively in $u$ and $v$; the boundary terms tend to zero as the rectangles expand because of Gaussian decay and the growth bound. The same integrable majorant and [F10] pass the rectangle limits, giving $\partial_\rho E[g(U)g(V)]=\sqrt{st}E[g'(U)g'(V)]$. Its absolute value is at most $QL^2$ for $g=\sigma$ and $Q\beta^2$ for $g=\sigma'$, since $|\sigma'|\le L$ and $|\sigma''|\le\beta$. At $\rho=\pm1$, the representation $U=\sqrt s Z$, $V=\sqrt t(\rho Z+\sqrt{1-\rho^2}Z')$ is dominated after multiplication by either pair of activations by $C(1+|Z|+|Z'|)^2$, which is integrable; [F10] gives continuity at both endpoints. Finally $\rho=Q_{ij}/\sqrt{st}$ is Lipschitz in the covariance entries when $s,t\ge v$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra]

Thus the nonnegative square-root map is increasing. It is continuous at every $x_0>0$, since $\sqrt x+\sqrt{x_0}\ge\sqrt{x_0}>0$ and $$|\sqrt x-\sqrt{x_0}|=\frac{|x-x_0|}{\sqrt x+\sqrt{x_0}}\le\frac{|x-x_0|}{\sqrt{x_0}};$$ given $\varepsilon>0$, $|x-x_0|<\varepsilon\sqrt{x_0}$ makes this difference less than $\varepsilon$. At $x_0=0$, for each $\varepsilon>0$, $0\le x<\varepsilon^2$ implies $\sqrt x<\sqrt{\varepsilon^2}=\varepsilon$, so it is continuous there as well. The map $u\mapsto u_+$ is nondecreasing and continuous, since $|u_+-v_+|\le|u-v|$ by its sign cases. Thus $a\sqrt{x}-2\sqrt L$ and its positive part are continuous, and [F15] makes the final composition defining $f$ continuous. The positive part is nonnegative and nondecreasing; for $0\le u\le v$, $v^2-u^2=(v-u)(v+u)\ge0$, so squaring preserves that order. Hence the exponent is nonincreasing, and [F14] makes $f$ nonincreasing; its exponent is nonpositive, so positivity, monotonicity and $\exp(0)=1$ give $0<f\le1$. The continuous function $f$ is integrable on $[0,n-1]$ by [F16], and repeated use of [F17] gives $\int_0^{n-1} f=\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}\int_{s-1}^s f$.
